newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: MINISTER DETERMINED TO SOLVE BLACK DEATHS PROBLEM
Federal Aborginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, says he's determined to find answers to reduce indigenous deaths in custody.
A summit involving 20 State and Territory Ministers and 14 Indigenous leaders has begun in Canberra after months of delay.
Senator Herron says $400-million has been spent trying to resolve the problem with little impact.
He says this Summit is different because governments have come to listen to indigenous people.
Senator Herron says he's optimistic all parties will agree on a final communique by the end of the day.
He says Australia has made achievements on many problems, such as the AIDS epidemic, and there's no reason why the country can't achieve an outcome on black deaths in custody.
HERRON NOT WORRIED ABOUT MANDATORY SENTENCING BUT LAWYERS ARE
Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron says he's not concerned about the impact of the Northern Territory's mandatory sentencing laws on Aboriginal deaths in custody.
Federal, State, and Territory indigenous leaders and Attorneys General today are attending a Canberra summit on black deaths in custody, and the lack of progress since the Royal Commission.
Senator Herron told ABC radio the Territory must be doing something right and the Federal Government wants to find out what that is.
He says there has been a very small number of deaths in custody in the Northern Territory despite its Mandatory Sentencing law.
But the Northern Territory Criminal Lawyers Association claims a death will occur in a Territory Jail somewhere due to Mandatory Sentencing Laws.
The Associations' John Tippett says while Australia is talking about how to reduce Aboriginal incarceration rates the Territory has a law which will increase the number of Aborigines in jail.
He says it's inevitable that if more Aboriginal people are put in jail more often there will be more deaths in prison.
Mr Tippett says somebody who should never have been in prison will die in custody at some stage, because of the regime.
WHITLAM PICKS DEANE FOR PRESIDENT
Former Prime Minister Gough Whitlam says the current Governor-General, Sir William Deane, would be an ideal first President for Australia.
Speaking on Classic-FM, Mr Whitlam says he's not happy at the prospect of the Queen opening the Sydney Olympics in the year 2000, because she will be representing Britain, not Australia.
But he says under the current Olympics rules, there's no other choice.
Mr Whitlam says says Australia has never had a better Governor-General than Sir William Deane.
But he says other countries do no accept Sir William as Australia's Head of State.
"That's no reflection on Sir William Deane. I mean I think he would make an ideal President. I would like him if I may so to be the first President," Mr Whitlam said.
MINE PICKETERS TRY TO STOP TRAIN
Coal miners on a picket line at the Hunter Valley number one mine near Singleton, will this morning attempt to stop a train from leaving the mine loaded with coal extracted by non union staff.

Picket lines in front of the mine have been staffed for four weeks and it's expected that members of the Public Transport Union will refuse to drive the train through the line. Mine General Manager Allan Davies says the train will arrive at the loading point and he's hopeful there will be some assistance from the management of Freight Rail in order to honour their contracts.
WOOMERA POISED FOR "ALIEN" INVASION
The South Australian outback defence town of Woomera is getting ready for an alien invasion.
But it's all part of today's Independence Day celebrations. The town's American and Australian residents are celebrating the 4th of July with an "intergalactic" theme.
In the school parade, students will dress as aliens and bring to life characters from their favourite space movies.
The outerspace theme continues on Saturday night with the Independence Day Intergalactic Ball.

Lieutenant Colonel George Reader says there's also fireworks and a unique "Smallest America's Cup" competition with teams building boats from cardboard and plastic, negotiating a deep pit of mud for a chance to win the Cup.
WHEELCHAIR PROTEST OUTSIDE PM'S OFFICE
In Sydney, there has been a stand-off between protesters in wheelchairs and armed guards, outside the Prime Minister's office.
About 70 people with various physical and intellectual disabilities were demonstrating against budget cuts to the Human Rights and Equal Opportunities Comission
They tried to send a delagation into the Commonwealth Offices Building but a spokesman found the way was barred by three guards.
Federal Government staff relented and allowed one protester in a wheelchair to enter the building to arrange a meeting with the Prime Minister's staff.
